title: The Pencil Nebula: Remnants of an Exploded Star (NGC 2736)
caption: Part of the Pencil Nebula (NGC 2736), imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Pencil Nebula, NGC 2736 · constellation Vela · about About 815 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: Wispy filaments, small bright knots and patches of diffuse gas cross this view of the Pencil Nebula from upper left to lower right in shades of orange and green. Catalogued as NGC 2736, the nebula is a small part of the huge Vela supernova remnant, about 815 light-years away in the southern constellation Vela. Hubble is looking along the edge of a rippled sheet of gas, and the patch shown spans about three fourths of a light-year.

The sheet appears to be part of the supernova's shock wave, which recently ran into a pocket of dense gas. As the shock moves through space, from right to left in the picture, it heats the gas it hits to millions of degrees. The gas then cools and gives off visible light. Its colour tracks temperature. NASA describes the hottest regions as dominated by ionized oxygen, shown in blue, and cooler regions as glowing red with hydrogen.
Sir John Herschel discovered the nebula in the 1840s, and its long, straight look earned it its popular name.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys took the image. NASA's release says ionized oxygen appears blue and hydrogen red, but the full filter-to-colour mapping is not published.
understand.eye: The colours sort the gas by temperature, and a 3-hour exposure gathers much more light than the eye can.

behind.people: See full credit: NASA, Hubble Heritage Project
behind.exposure: Observation dates per NASA: October 21, 2002, Exposure Time: 3 hours.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: A spinning pulsar remains at the heart of the Vela region. From how fast it is slowing, astronomers estimate the explosion may have happened about 11,000 years ago. No historical record of it survives, but it would have outshone Venus 250 times over and been visible to southern observers in daylight. If that age is right, the blast flung material out at nearly 22 million miles per hour, and the Pencil Nebula now moves at roughly 400,000 miles per hour.
sources: NASA release: Supernova Shock Wave Paints Cosmic Portrait
alt: Wispy filaments of gas in shades of orange and green crossing the frame from upper left to lower right.
